subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Cooling: The Forgotten Step
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Cooling: The Forgotten Step.

hook.text: After roasting stops, the beans are still 200°C+. If not cooled fast, they continue cooking—ruining the roast profile.

buildup.text: Cooling trays blast ambient air through the hot beans, dropping temperature from 200°C to room temp in 3–5 minutes.

discovery.text: Beans must cool to under 40°C within 4 minutes. Slow cooling adds unwanted development time and dulls acidity.

twist.text: Some roasters use water quenching—spraying a fine mist onto hot beans. It's faster but adds weight and risks moisture damage.

climax.text: The cooling step effectively ends the roast. A perfect profile can be ruined by slow or uneven cooling alone.

punchline.text: Roasting doesn't end when heat stops. It ends when the bean is cool.

quiz.question: Why must roasted beans be cooled quickly?
options: To make them easier to package
Still-hot beans continue cooking, ruining the intended roast profile

details.summary: Cooling stops the roast by rapidly dropping bean temperature within a few minutes. If cooling is too slow, residual heat continues development and pushes the roast darker than intended. Most commercial roasters use a cooling tray with fans to halt the process.
details.whyItMatters: Proper cooling preserves the exact flavor profile the roaster intended. Slow cooling is one of the most common causes of inconsistent batch quality.
takeaways: Beans must cool quickly to stop residual heat from over-roasting
Cooling trays with fans bring temperature down within minutes
Delayed cooling shifts the roast profile darker than planned

faq.question: How quickly should roasted coffee beans be cooled?
faq.answer: Best practice is to cool beans to near room temperature within four to five minutes of dropping them from the roaster. Some commercial systems achieve this in under three minutes using powerful fans.

faq.question: Is water quenching a good method for cooling roasted coffee?
faq.answer: Water quenching is used by some large commercial roasters to speed cooling, but it can add moisture back into the bean and affect shelf life. Most specialty roasters prefer air cooling for cleaner results.
